A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Epsilon-Scheduling study. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite reformatting and table renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original robust fine-tuning experiments, comparisons across backbones and datasets, AutoAttack evaluations, and scheduling ablations in the main text and Appendices B–C.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds automatic-scheduler evaluations, ImageNette results, and statistical analyses.

M1.justification: Section 6.3 adds an automatic scheduling variant: validation-accuracy convergence selects T1, followed by a linear perturbation increase through the remaining training. The original two-hinge scheduler, adversarial objective, and model architectures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix E and Table 12 add ImageNette classification evaluations with SWIN and CNX at 4/255 and 8/255. The five original downstream datasets and their tasks are retained.

E2.justification: New Table 4 adds auto as an evaluated scheduling comparator alongside fix and sched on Aircraft, Caltech, and Cars. Existing comparisons remain. Expanded discussion of TWINS, AutoLoRA, and RoLi does not introduce evaluations of those methods.

E3.justification: The added automatic-scheduler experiment introduces validation-dependent timing, using five-epoch patience and 2% tolerance, with the ramp continuing to training completion. Existing experiments retain their splits, preprocessing, 50-epoch budget, APGD training/evaluation steps, and accuracy metrics.

E4.justification: Section 6.3 and Table 4 add a targeted test of whether validation-based timing can replace manually selected schedule boundaries. The original T1/T2 sensitivity sweeps, uniform-sampling comparison, robust-backbone analysis, and AutoAttack checks are retained.

E5.justification: v1 provides no significance tests. New Appendix D and Table 9 introduce paired t-tests covering all three principal metrics at both perturbation budgets, with 30 paired model–dataset configurations per test. This adds formal statistical assessment across the central comparison; it does not establish additional training runs or report seed-level uncertainty.

E6.justification: The original numerical result tables are unchanged. Table 4 adds auto results, with expected robustness below sched in all 12 configurations. Table 12 adds ImageNette results; for example, SWIN at 8/255 has expected robustness 86.93 for scheduler versus 82.43 for fix. Tables 9–11 add statistical outcomes and numerical averages. Table 10 contains a small inconsistency: ViT-fix clean accuracy at 8/255 averages to 15.52 from Table 2, versus the reported 15.59.

T1.justification: The adversarial-risk, scheduling, expected-robustness, and numerical-integration equations are retained. The added Dirac-distribution endpoint example explains the existing metric; the new theoretical open questions supply no theorem, proof, or substantive derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution summary, and conclusion retain the same central claims about suboptimal transfer, delayed adaptation, Epsilon-Scheduling, and expected robustness. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining their scientific scope.

C2.justification: The expanded limitations explicitly question whether delayed adaptation is the sole cause of suboptimal transfer and identify unresolved mechanisms and relevant pretraining properties. Section 6.3 also interprets automatic scheduling as effective despite lower expected robustness than the manually specified scheduler.

D1.justification: v1 mentions a code repository without giving the study's repository address. v2 adds an explicit link and a reproducibility statement describing implementation, HPO results, figure/table data, reproduction scripts, and setup instructions. It also specifies the automatic scheduler's patience and tolerance. Existing Appendix A implementation and compute details remain.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands the discussion of TWINS, AutoLoRA, and RoLi to explain their reported reliance on robust pretraining. Section 6.3 changes the linear-warmup attribution from Cao et al. to Debenedetti et al. The bibliography and principal novelty positioning otherwise remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The title replaces Adversarial Scheduling with Epsilon-Scheduling, and v2 makes local wording and affiliation edits. It adds short discussions, a reproducibility statement, and Appendices D–E while retaining most prose and the original section sequence.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICLR presentation with redesigned front matter and running headers, relocates figures and tables throughout the document, and adds five tables: automatic scheduling, significance tests, two aggregate summaries, and ImageNette results. All twelve original figures remain; original appendix tables are renumbered rather than removed.

improvement.justification: v2 improves practical usefulness and transparency through the evaluated automatic scheduler, ImageNette extension, explicit reproduction-resource disclosure, and more specific mechanistic limitations. Statistical tests add analysis of the retained benchmark results, although they do not quantify training-seed variability. These benefits outweigh the small averaging inconsistency in new Table 10, but the unchanged central evidence and limited scope of the extensions support a minor overall improvement.
